title: Effect of the intensity of light on an LDR
objective: To measure how the resistance of an LDR changes as a lamp is moved away from it.
To combine the inverse-square law with the photoconductive power law.
To find the exponent γ of the cell from the slope of a log-log graph.

theory.statement: The resistance of a cadmium-sulphide cell falls as the light on it rises, following R = A·E^(−γ), where E is the illuminance and γ is between about 0.7 and 0.9. The illuminance from a small lamp obeys the inverse-square law, E = I/d². Substituting gives R ∝ d^(2γ), so a graph of log R against log d is a straight line whose slope is 2γ. This is how γ can be found without ever measuring illuminance directly: the distance is the quantity a school laboratory can measure accurately, and the two power laws chain together to give the answer.
keyEquations: Photoconductivity: absorbed photons free charge carriers, so resistance falls as light rises.
E = I/d² for a point source, so doubling the distance quarters the illuminance.
R = A·E^(−γ) gives R ∝ d^(2γ) once the two are combined.
The slope of log R against log d is 2γ, so γ is half the slope.
Ambient light adds to the illuminance and flattens the far end of the graph.

apparatus.name: LDR (cadmium sulphide cell)
apparatus.why: The component under study; its resistance depends on the light falling on it.

apparatus.name: Lamp on an optical bench
apparatus.why: A small source whose distance can be varied and measured.

apparatus.name: Metre scale along the bench
apparatus.why: Distance is the independent variable and must be measured accurately.

apparatus.name: Digital multimeter on the ohms range
apparatus.why: Reads the cell resistance without passing enough current to heat it.

apparatus.name: Blackout screen
apparatus.why: Excludes room light, which would otherwise add to the illuminance and spoil the graph.

procedure: Mount the LDR facing the lamp along the bench, and black out the room.
Set the lamp at the nearest distance and allow the cell a few seconds to settle.
Read the resistance on the ohmmeter and record it against the distance.
Move the lamp outwards in steps, taking a reading at each position.
Cover a wide range of distance: the furthest should be at least three times the nearest.
Plot log R against log d, draw the best straight line, and take γ as half its slope.

steps: For each reading compute log d and log R.
Plot log R on the vertical axis against log d on the horizontal.
Draw the best straight line and measure its slope.
The slope equals 2γ, so γ is half the slope.
Compare γ with the accepted range of 0.7 to 0.9 for cadmium sulphide.

expectedResult.statement: The resistance rises steadily as the lamp is moved away, and a log-log plot is a straight line. Its slope is 2γ, giving γ between about 0.7 and 0.9 for a cadmium-sulphide cell. In a blacked-out room the fit is excellent. With the room lights on, the ambient illuminance adds to that from the lamp, the far end of the graph flattens, and the slope — and hence γ — comes out substantially too small even though the procedure was followed correctly.

safety: The lamp becomes hot: allow it to cool before moving it, and do not touch the envelope.
Do not look directly into the lamp at short distances.
Keep the mains lead clear of the hot lamp housing.
sourcesOfError: Room light adding to the illuminance, which flattens the graph and lowers the fitted γ.
Using too narrow a range of distance, so the slope is poorly determined.
Working too close to the lamp, where a bulb of finite size is not a point source.
Not allowing the cell to settle: an LDR drifts for several seconds after a change in light.
Heating of the cell by the lamp, since CdS resistance falls by about 0.4 % per degree.
The cell not facing the lamp squarely, so the illuminance is reduced by a cosine factor.

viva.question: Why does the resistance of an LDR fall when light falls on it?
viva.expectedConcept: Photons with energy above the band gap free charge carriers, so conductivity rises.
viva.answerLogic: Photons with energy above the band gap free charge carriers, so conductivity rises.
viva.commonMisconception: That the light heats the cell and that is why the resistance changes.

viva.question: What is the relation between illuminance and distance from a small lamp?
viva.commonMisconception: That illuminance falls in proportion to the distance.

viva.question: Why is log R plotted against log d rather than R against d?
viva.expectedConcept: A power law becomes a straight line on log-log axes, and the slope gives the exponent.
viva.answerLogic: A power law becomes a straight line on log-log axes, and the slope gives the exponent.
viva.commonMisconception: That the log axes are only for fitting large numbers on the page.

viva.question: The slope of the log-log line is 1.44. What is γ?
viva.expectedConcept: 0.72, since the slope is 2γ — one factor of γ from the cell and a factor of two from the inverse-square law.
viva.answerLogic: 0.72, since the slope is 2γ — one factor of γ from the cell and a factor of two from the inverse-square law.
viva.commonMisconception: That the slope is γ itself.

viva.question: Why does room light spoil the experiment?
viva.expectedConcept: The cell responds to the total illuminance; once ambient light dominates, moving the lamp changes little and the graph flattens.
viva.answerLogic: The cell responds to the total illuminance; once ambient light dominates, moving the lamp changes little and the graph flattens.
viva.commonMisconception: That a constant background simply shifts the line without changing its slope.

viva.question: Would the error from room light make γ too large or too small?
viva.expectedConcept: Too small, because the far points lie above the true line and reduce the slope.
viva.answerLogic: Too small, because the far points lie above the true line and reduce the slope.
viva.commonMisconception: That a systematic error is equally likely either way.

viva.question: Why must the lamp not be too close to the cell?
viva.expectedConcept: The inverse-square law assumes a point source; close up the filament has an appreciable size.
viva.answerLogic: The inverse-square law assumes a point source; close up the filament has an appreciable size.
viva.commonMisconception: That the law holds at all distances.

viva.question: Why should the cell be allowed to settle before each reading?
viva.expectedConcept: An LDR has a slow and asymmetric response and drifts for seconds after a change in light.
viva.answerLogic: An LDR has a slow and asymmetric response and drifts for seconds after a change in light.

viva.question: Give one practical use of an LDR.
viva.expectedConcept: Switching street lights at dusk, or automatic exposure control in a camera.
viva.answerLogic: Switching street lights at dusk, or automatic exposure control in a camera.
viva.commonMisconception: That an LDR measures light precisely enough for a lux meter.

viva.question: Why is an LDR poor for precise measurement of illuminance?
viva.expectedConcept: Its response is a slow power law that varies widely between cells and drifts with temperature.
viva.answerLogic: Its response is a slow power law that varies widely between cells and drifts with temperature.
viva.commonMisconception: That any component with a measurable response makes a good instrument.
